demographics: Much more common in men because benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer obstruct the outlet
Incidence rises steadily with age in men
In women it is uncommon and usually follows pelvic surgery or a gynecologic cause

risk_factors.text: Spinal cord injury or neurologic disease

comorbidities: Spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis
social_history: Long-standing lower urinary tract symptoms that were tolerated without treatment

chief_complaints.text: My lower belly is hurting and feels like it's going to burst
I keep feeling like I need to go but nothing comes out

hpi.onset: Sudden, over minutes to a few hours
hpi.duration: Hours; most present within 12–24 hours of being unable to void
hpi.progression: Complete inability to pass any urine, with steadily worsening suprapubic pain and a growing sense of fullness; some patients dribble small amounts but never feel emptied
hpi.radiation: Usually none; severe cases may feel pressure radiating to the back or perineum
hpi.quality: Constant, dull to sharp pressure and pain
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; often 7–10/10 at presentation

atypical.how_it_differs: May report little pain and present with confusion, agitation or a fall rather than a clear inability to void.

atypical.how_it_differs: A retroverted gravid uterus can cause retention in the first trimester; in later pregnancy the presenting part may compress the outlet.
Autonomic neuropathy can cause a painless, atonic bladder that retains large volumes with little discomfort.

labs.caveat: Obstructive nephropathy from back-pressure; a normal creatinine does not exclude retention, and values fall quickly after decompression.
Rises with the creatinine; a high BUN/creatinine ratio also reflects dehydration and poor intake.
Hyperkalemia from acute kidney injury is the main immediate danger; check before and after decompression.
Metabolic acidosis accompanying the obstructive kidney injury.
Hyponatremia is uncommon and usually reflects free-water retention or a coexisting cause.
Leukocytosis suggests a complicating urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis rather than retention alone.
Leukocyte esterase is often positive from sterile inflammation of a distended bladder, so it does not by itself prove infection.
A positive nitrite points to a true gram-negative urinary infection complicating the retention.
Pyuria can be sterile; correlate with nitrite and culture.
Microscopic hematuria from bladder overdistension or from an underlying stone or tumor.
Negative. Required in any woman of childbearing age before imaging or instrumentation; a retroverted gravid uterus is a cause of retention.

decision_points: Confirm a distended bladder at the bedside before catheterization
Decompress the bladder promptly with a urethral or suprapubic catheter; monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and hematuria
Check potassium and creatinine before and after decompression because obstructive acute kidney injury can cause dangerous hyperkalemia
Pregnancy test before imaging or instrumentation in anyone who could be pregnant
Look for red flags of cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, loss of bowel control) and image the spine urgently if present

differential.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differential.why_considered: Inability to void with a full bladder can be the presenting feature of a compressive lesion of the cauda equina
differential.trigger: Saddle anesthesia, lower extremity weakness, or loss of bowel control alongside retention

history: Progressive low back pain radiating to both legs
Numbness in the groin, perineum or inner thighs
Loss of bowel control or fecal incontinence
Recent heavy lifting or known lumbar disc disease
exam: Reduced or absent sensation in the saddle distribution
Weakness of the lower extremities
Reduced or absent anal sphincter tone
Absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes in the legs
labs: No specific laboratory abnormality; workup is imaging-driven
imaging: MRI lumbar spine showing disc herniation, mass or hematoma compressing the cauda equina

differential.name: Acute pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Fever, dysuria and lower urinary tract symptoms with flank pain can accompany difficulty voiding
differential.trigger: Fever with chills and flank pain rather than isolated suprapubic pressure

history: Fever and chills
Unilateral flank pain
Nausea and vomiting
Dysuria and frequency preceding the pain
exam: Costovertebral angle tenderness
Temperature above 100.4°F
No firm suprapubic mass; bladder may not be distended
labs: Positive nitrite and leukocyte esterase on urinalysis
Urine culture growing a gram-negative organism
Creatinine usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: CT or ultrasound showing focal renal inflammation; bladder not distended

differential.name: Urinary tract infection without retention
differential.why_considered: Dysuria, urgency and frequency can mimic the irritative symptoms of retention

history: Burning with urination
Passing small frequent volumes rather than none at all
No sense of a painfully full bladder
exam: No firm suprapubic mass
Suprapubic tenderness may be present but bladder is not distended
imaging: Bladder ultrasound shows a small post-void residual

differential.name: Urinary incontinence
differential.why_considered: Involuntary leakage of urine can be mistaken for inability to void, especially with overflow dribbling

history: Leakage with coughing, sneezing or urgency rather than complete inability to pass urine
Able to initiate a stream, even if weak
No severe suprapubic pain
exam: Bladder not palpable or only mildly distended
Positive cough stress test in stress incontinence
imaging: Post-void residual is small, typically under 100 mL

differential.name: Bladder outlet obstruction from urethral stricture
differential.why_considered: Progressive narrowing of the urethra can cause acute retention with a distended bladder

history: Long-standing weak stream and straining
History of urethral trauma, instrumentation or sexually transmitted infection
No prior prostate symptoms
exam: Palpable distended bladder
Difficulty passing a urethral catheter; a firm urethral ridge may be felt
labs: Elevated creatinine if obstruction has caused kidney injury
imaging: Retrograde urethrogram showing a narrowed urethral segment
Ultrasound showing a distended bladder with a thin stream on voiding

differential.name: Fecal impaction
differential.why_considered: A large stool burden in the rectum can compress the bladder outlet and cause retention, especially in older adults

history: Constipation with no bowel movement for days
Chronic laxative use or opioid therapy
Abdominal bloating and overflow diarrhea
exam: Hard stool palpable on digital rectal exam
Distended bladder may also be present
Abdomen may be tympanitic with a palpable stool mass
labs: No specific abnormality; may show dehydration
imaging: Abdominal x-ray or CT showing a large fecal burden in the rectum and colon

differential.name: Neurogenic bladder from diabetic autonomic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: An atonic bladder from autonomic neuropathy can present with painless retention and large residual volumes

history: Long-standing diabetes mellitus
Painless inability to void or insidious onset
Other neuropathic symptoms such as numbness or erectile dysfunction
exam: Distended bladder may be present but with little tenderness
Reduced sensation in the feet
Normal prostate on rectal exam
imaging: Bladder ultrasound showing a large post-void residual with a smooth, thin-walled bladder

differential.name: Prostate cancer
differential.why_considered: Locally advanced prostate cancer can obstruct the bladder outlet and cause acute retention

history: Progressive weak stream and nocturia
Bone pain, especially in the back or hips
Weight loss
exam: Hard, irregular or asymmetric prostate nodule on digital rectal exam
Palpable bladder
Lymphadenopathy or bone tenderness
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase if bone metastases are present
imaging: MRI prostate showing a suspicious lesion
Bone scan or CT showing metastases

severity.mild: Able to pass small amounts with straining, suprapubic discomfort, bladder palpable but not tense, no systemic symptoms, normal creatinine
severity.moderate: Complete inability to void for several hours, firm tender suprapubic mass, marked restlessness, mild creatinine elevation, no fever
severity.severe: Many hours of complete retention with severe pain, guarding, rising creatinine and hyperkalemia, may have fever if infection is complicating
severity.critical: Retention with obstructive acute kidney injury and dangerous hyperkalemia, sepsis from infected retained urine, or bladder rupture with peritoneal signs

red_flags.finding: Saddle anesthesia, lower extremity weakness or loss of bowel control
red_flags.meaning: Cauda equina syndrome; needs urgent MRI and neurosurgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever with chills and flank pain
red_flags.meaning: Complicating pyelonephritis or urosepsis; needs cultures and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Hyperkalemia with peaked T waves or widened QRS on ECG
red_flags.meaning: Obstructive acute kidney injury is life-threatening; needs immediate decompression and potassium management
May indicate bladder tumor, stone or trauma; needs urologic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Diffuse abdominal rigidity or rebound tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Possible bladder rupture or peritonitis; surgical emergency
Sepsis or severe obstructive nephropathy; resuscitate and decompress

complications.name: Post-obstructive diuresis
clues: Urine output over 200 mL per hour after decompression

complications.name: Recurrent retention and chronic bladder decompensation

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, agitation or a fall rather than pain; retention is often precipitated by anticholinergic or opioid medications and by constipation.
Often presents with crying, irritability, abdominal mass or urinary dribbling; causes include posterior urethral valves, stones and neurologic disease.
A retroverted gravid uterus can cause retention in the first trimester; in later pregnancy the presenting part may compress the outlet. Pregnancy test is required before imaging or instrumentation.
Autonomic neuropathy can cause a painless, atonic bladder with large residual volumes and little discomfort; infection risk is higher.
Obstructive nephropathy can cause rapid creatinine rise and hyperkalemia; monitor electrolytes closely before and after decompression.

key_questions.question: When was the last time you were able to pass any urine at all?
key_questions.looking_for: Complete inability to void for hours; distinguishes acute retention from chronic retention with overflow

key_questions.question: Are you passing any urine at all, even a few drops?
key_questions.looking_for: No urine or only dribbling overflow; complete retention versus partial voiding

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and how bad is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe suprapubic pressure and pain, often 7-10/10, unrelieved by anything

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble with your stream, straining, or getting up at night to urinate before this?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing lower urinary tract symptoms suggesting benign prostatic hyperplasia

key_questions.question: Do you feel like your bladder is still full after you try to go?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensation of incomplete emptying and a firm, swollen lower belly

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or burning when you do pass a few drops?
key_questions.looking_for: Complicating urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis

key_questions.question: Have you had any numbness in the groin or inner thighs, weakness in your legs, or loss of bowel control?
key_questions.looking_for: Saddle anesthesia, leg weakness or fecal incontinence suggesting cauda equina syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent pelvic, prostate or bladder surgery, or a catheter placed?
key_questions.looking_for: Postoperative retention or urethral instrumentation as the cause

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, multiple sclerosis, a spinal cord injury, or other neurologic disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurogenic bladder as the underlying cause

key_questions.question: Have you taken any antihistamines, cold medicines, bladder medicines, antidepressants, or pain medicines like opioids recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergic, sympathomimetic or opioid medications precipitating retention

key_questions.question: When was your last bowel movement? Do you have trouble with constipation?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation or fecal impaction compressing the bladder outlet

key_questions.question: Have you had any blood in your urine, or passed clots?
key_questions.looking_for: Gross hematuria suggesting tumor, stone or trauma

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: A retroverted gravid uterus as a cause and to guide imaging and instrumentation

reasoning_points: Sudden, painful inability to pass any urine over hours, with a firm, tender suprapubic mass
A palpable or percussible distended bladder confirmed at the bedside by ultrasound with a large post-void residual
Preceding lower urinary tract symptoms such as weak stream, straining and nocturia pointing to benign prostatic hyperplasia
A precipitating medication, recent pelvic or urologic surgery, constipation or a neurologic cause identified on history
Red flags for cauda equina syndrome, complicating infection or obstructive kidney injury specifically sought and excluded
Elevated creatinine and potassium from obstructive nephropathy, with hyperkalemia as the immediate danger
Pregnancy excluded in a woman of childbearing age before imaging or instrumentation
Look-alikes such as urinary tract infection, urinary incontinence and pyelonephritis distinguished by the absence of a distended bladder or by fever and flank pain

Bedside bladder ultrasound shows a large post-void residual

Constipation or fecal impaction found on rectal exam as the cause
Mild creatinine elevation with a normal temperature

Retention with fever and flank pain suggesting complicating pyelonephritis or urosepsis
